16.3.oldText: The first few days of the voyage passed prosperously, amid favorable weather and propitious winds, and they soon came in sight of the great Andaman, the principal island in the Bay of Bengal, with its picturesque Saddle Peak, two thousand four hundred feet high, looming above the waters. The steamer passed close to the shores, but the savage Papuans, who are at the lowest scale of humanity, but are not, as has been claimed, cannibals, did not make their appearance.

16.4.oldText: The panorama of the islands, as they steamed by them, was superb. Vast forests of palms, arecs, bamboo, teakwood, of the gigantic mimosa and tree-like ferns, covered the foreground, while behind them the graceful outlines of the mountains were traced against the sky; and along the coasts swarmed by the thousands the precious swallows whose nests furnish a luxurious dish for the tables of the Celestial Empire. The varied landscape offered by the Andaman Islands was soon left behind, however, and the "Rangoon" was rapidly nearing the Straits of Malacca, which gave access to the China seas.

16.5.oldText: What was detective Fix, so unluckily drawn on from country to country, doing all this time? He had managed to embark on the "Rangoon" at Calcutta without being seen by Passepartout, after leaving orders that if the warrant should arrive, it should be forwarded to him at Hong Kong; and he hoped to keep his presence concealed to the end of the voyage. It would have been difficult to explain why he was on board without rousing Passepartout's suspicions, since Passepartout believed he was still at Bombay. But necessity drove him, nevertheless, to renew his acquaintance with the worthy servant, as will be seen.

16.6.oldText: All the detective's hopes and wishes now centered on Hong Kong; for the steamer's stay at Singapore would be too brief to allow him to take any steps there. The arrest must be made at Hong Kong, or the robber would probably escape him forever. Hong Kong was the last English ground on which he would set foot; beyond it, China, Japan, and America offered Fogg an almost certain refuge. If the warrant should at last turn up at Hong Kong, Fix could arrest him and hand him over to the local police, and there would be no further trouble. But beyond Hong Kong, a simple warrant would be of no use; an extradition warrant would be needed, and that would mean delays and obstacles of which the rascal would take advantage to slip away from justice.

16.7.oldText: Fix turned these probabilities over in his mind during the long hours he spent in his cabin, and kept repeating to himself, "Now, either the warrant will be at Hong Kong, in which case I shall arrest my man, or it will not be there; and this time it is absolutely necessary that I delay his departure. I have failed at Bombay, and I have failed at Calcutta; if I fail at Hong Kong, my reputation is lost. Cost what it may, I _must_ succeed! But how shall I prevent his departure, if that should turn out to be my last resource?"

16.8.oldText: Fix made up his mind that, if the worst came to the worst, he would take Passepartout into his confidence and tell him what kind of fellow his master really was. That Passepartout was not Fogg's accomplice he was quite sure. The servant, enlightened by his disclosure and afraid of being himself implicated in the crime, would no doubt become an ally of the detective. But this method was a dangerous one, only to be used when everything else had failed. A single word from Passepartout to his master would ruin everything. The detective was therefore in a tight spot. But suddenly a new idea struck him. The presence of Aouda on the "Rangoon," in the company of Phileas Fogg, gave him new material for reflection.

16.9.oldText: Who was this woman? What combination of events had made her Fogg's traveling companion? They had evidently met somewhere between Bombay and Calcutta; but where? Had they met by chance, or had Fogg gone into the interior on purpose in quest of this charming damsel? Fix was fairly puzzled. He asked himself whether there had not been a wicked elopement; and this idea so impressed itself upon his mind that he determined to make use of the supposed intrigue. Whether the young woman were married or not, he would be able to create such difficulties for Mr. Fogg at Hong Kong that he could not escape by paying any amount of money.

16.10.oldText: But could he even wait until they reached Hong Kong? Fogg had an abominable way of jumping from one boat to another, and before anything could be done he might be fully under way again for Yokohama.

16.11.oldText: Fix decided he must warn the English authorities and signal the "Rangoon" before her arrival. This was easy to do, since the steamer stopped at Singapore, from which there is a telegraph wire to Hong Kong. Moreover, before acting more decisively, he finally resolved to question Passepartout. It would not be hard to make him talk; and, as there was no time to lose, Fix prepared to make himself known.

16.12.oldText: It was now the 30th of October, and on the following day the "Rangoon" was due at Singapore.

16.13.oldText: Fix came out of his cabin and went on deck. Passepartout was strolling up and down in the forward part of the steamer. The detective rushed forward with every appearance of extreme surprise, and exclaimed, "You here, on the 'Rangoon'?"

16.14.oldText: "What, Monsieur Fix, are you on board?" replied the genuinely astonished Passepartout, recognizing his crony of the "Mongolia." "Why, I left you at Bombay, and here you are, on the way to Hong Kong! Are you going round the world too?"

16.15.oldText: "No, no," replied Fix; "I shall stop at Hong Kong—at least for some days."

16.16.oldText: "Hum!" said Passepartout, who seemed for an instant perplexed. "But how is it I haven't seen you on board since we left Calcutta?"

16.17.oldText: "Oh, a trifle of seasickness—I've been staying in my berth. The Gulf of Bengal doesn't agree with me as well as the Indian Ocean. And how is Mr. Fogg?"

16.18.oldText: "As well and as punctual as ever, not a day behind time! But, Monsieur Fix, you don't know that we have a young lady with us."

16.19.oldText: "A young lady?" replied the detective, not seeming to understand what was said.

16.20.oldText: Passepartout thereupon recounted Aouda's history—the affair at the Bombay pagoda, the purchase of the elephant for two thousand pounds, the rescue, the arrest, and the sentence of the Calcutta court, and the release of Mr. Fogg and himself on bail. Fix, who was familiar with the latter events, seemed equally ignorant of everything Passepartout related; and the latter was charmed to find so interested a listener.

16.21.oldText: "But does your master mean to take this young woman to Europe?"

16.22.oldText: "Not at all. We are simply going to place her under the protection of one of her relatives, a rich merchant at Hong Kong."

16.23.oldText: "Nothing to be done there," Fix said to himself, hiding his disappointment. "A glass of gin, Mr. Passepartout?"

16.24.oldText: "Willingly, Monsieur Fix. We must at least have a friendly glass on board the 'Rangoon.'"

18.0.oldText: The weather was bad during the latter days of the voyage. The wind, obstinately holding in the north-west, blew a gale and held the steamer back. The "Rangoon" rolled heavily, and the passengers grew impatient with the long, monstrous waves that the wind raised across their path. A sort of tempest came up on the 3rd of November, the squall knocking the vessel about with fury and the waves running high. The "Rangoon" reefed all her sails, and even the rigging proved too much, whistling and shaking amid the squall. The steamer was forced to move slowly, and the captain estimated that she would reach Hong Kong twenty hours behind time, and more if the storm lasted.

18.1.oldText: Phileas Fogg gazed at the tempestuous sea—which seemed to be struggling especially to delay him—with his habitual tranquility. He never changed countenance for an instant, though a delay of twenty hours, by making him too late for the Yokohama boat, would almost inevitably mean the loss of the wager. But this man of nerve showed neither impatience nor annoyance; it was as if the storm were a part of his program and had been foreseen. Aouda was amazed to find him as calm as he had been from the first time she saw him.

18.2.oldText: Fix did not view the state of things in the same light. The storm pleased him greatly. His satisfaction would have been complete had the "Rangoon" been forced to retreat before the violence of wind and waves. Each delay filled him with hope, for it was becoming more and more probable that Fogg would have to remain some days at Hong Kong; and now the heavens themselves became his allies, with the gusts and squalls. It did not matter that they made him seasick—he took no account of this inconvenience; and, while his body was writhing under their effects, his spirit bounded with hopeful exultation.

18.3.oldText: Passepartout was enraged beyond words by the unpropitious weather. Everything had gone so well till now! Earth and sea had seemed to be at his master's service; steamers and railways obeyed him; wind and steam combined to speed his journey. Had the hour of adversity come? Passepartout was as worked up as if the twenty thousand pounds were to come out of his own pocket. The storm exasperated him, the gale made him furious, and he longed to lash the stubborn sea into obedience. Poor fellow! Fix carefully concealed his own satisfaction from him, for, had he betrayed it, Passepartout could scarcely have kept himself from personal violence.

18.4.oldText: Passepartout stayed on deck as long as the tempest lasted, unable to stay quiet below, and taking it into his head to help the ship along by lending a hand with the crew. He overwhelmed the captain, officers, and sailors—who could not help laughing at his impatience—with all sorts of questions. He wanted to know exactly how long the storm was going to last; whereupon he was referred to the barometer, which seemed to have no intention of rising. Passepartout shook it, but with no perceptible effect; for neither shaking nor maledictions could prevail on it to change its mind.

18.5.oldText: On the 4th, however, the sea grew calmer and the storm let up in violence; the wind veered to the south and was once more favorable. Passepartout cleared up with the weather. Some of the sails were unfurled, and the "Rangoon" resumed its most rapid speed. The time lost could not, however, be made up. Land was not sighted until five o'clock on the morning of the 6th; the steamer was due on the 5th. Phileas Fogg was twenty-four hours behind, and the Yokohama steamer would, of course, be missed.

18.6.oldText: The pilot came on board at six and took his place on the bridge to guide the "Rangoon" through the channels into the port of Hong Kong. Passepartout longed to ask him whether the steamer had left for Yokohama; but he dared not, for he wished to preserve the spark of hope that still remained till the last moment. He had confided his anxiety to Fix, who—the sly rascal!—tried to console him by saying that Mr. Fogg would be in time if he took the next boat; but this only put Passepartout in a passion.

18.7.oldText: Mr. Fogg, bolder than his servant, did not hesitate to approach the pilot and tranquilly ask him if he knew when a steamer would leave Hong Kong for Yokohama.

18.8.oldText: "At high tide tomorrow morning," answered the pilot.

18.9.oldText: "Ah!" said Mr. Fogg, without betraying any astonishment.

18.10.oldText: Passepartout, who heard what was said, would willingly have embraced the pilot, while Fix would have been glad to twist his neck.

18.11.oldText: "What is the steamer's name?" asked Mr. Fogg.

18.14.oldText: "Yes, sir; but they had to repair one of her boilers, and so her departure was put off till tomorrow."

18.15.oldText: "Thank you," returned Mr. Fogg, going mathematically down to the saloon.

18.16.oldText: Passepartout clasped the pilot's hand and shook it heartily in his delight, exclaiming, "Pilot, you are the best of good fellows!"

18.17.oldText: The pilot probably does not know to this day why his answers earned him this enthusiastic greeting. He remounted the bridge and guided the steamer through the flotilla of junks, tankas, and fishing boats that crowd the harbor of Hong Kong.

18.18.oldText: At one o'clock the "Rangoon" was at the quay, and the passengers were going ashore.

18.19.oldText: Chance had strangely favored Phileas Fogg, for if the "Carnatic" had not been forced to lie over for the repair of her boilers, she would have left on the 6th of November, and the passengers for Japan would have had to wait a week for the sailing of the next steamer. Mr. Fogg was, it is true, twenty-four hours behind his time; but this could not seriously imperil the rest of his tour.

18.20.oldText: The steamer that crossed the Pacific from Yokohama to San Francisco made a direct connection with the one from Hong Kong, and could not sail until the latter reached Yokohama; and if Mr. Fogg were twenty-four hours late on reaching Yokohama, this time would no doubt be easily made up on the twenty-two-day voyage across the Pacific. So he found himself about twenty-four hours behind time, thirty-five days after leaving London.

18.21.oldText: The "Carnatic" was announced to leave Hong Kong at five the next morning. Mr. Fogg had sixteen hours in which to attend to his business there, which was to deposit Aouda safely with her wealthy relative.

18.22.oldText: On landing, he conducted her to a palanquin, in which they made their way to the Club Hotel. A room was engaged for the young woman, and Mr. Fogg, after seeing that she wanted for nothing, set out in search of her cousin Jeejeeh. He instructed Passepartout to remain at the hotel until his return, so that Aouda would not be left entirely alone.

18.23.oldText: Mr. Fogg went to the Exchange, where, he had no doubt, everyone would know so wealthy and considerable a personage as the Parsee merchant. Meeting a broker, he made the inquiry, only to learn that Jeejeeh had left China two years before and, having retired from business with an immense fortune, had taken up his residence in Europe—in Holland, the broker thought, since it was with the merchants of that country that he had chiefly traded. Phileas Fogg returned to the hotel, asked for a moment's conversation with Aouda, and, without more ado, informed her that Jeejeeh was no longer at Hong Kong, but probably in Holland.

18.24.oldText: At first Aouda said nothing. She passed her hand across her forehead and reflected for a few moments. Then, in her sweet, soft voice, she said, "What ought I to do, Mr. Fogg?"

18.25.oldText: "It is very simple," replied the gentleman. "Go on to Europe."

18.27.oldText: "You do not intrude, nor do you in the least embarrass my project. Passepartout!"

18.29.oldText: "Go to the 'Carnatic,' and engage three cabins."

18.30.oldText: Passepartout, delighted that the young woman, who had been so gracious to him, was going to continue the journey with them, went off at a brisk pace to obey his master's order.

19.0.oldText: Hong Kong is an island that came into the possession of the English by the Treaty of Nankin, after the war of 1842; and the colonizing genius of the English has built on it an important city and an excellent port. The island lies at the mouth of the Canton River and is separated by about sixty miles from the Portuguese town of Macao on the opposite coast. Hong Kong has beaten Macao in the struggle for the Chinese trade, and now the greater part of the transportation of Chinese goods finds its depot at the former place. Docks, hospitals, wharves, a Gothic cathedral, a government house, macadamised streets, give to Hong Kong the appearance of a town in Kent or Surrey transferred by some strange magic to the antipodes.

19.1.oldText: Passepartout wandered, with his hands in his pockets, toward the Victoria port, gazing as he went at the curious palanquins and other modes of conveyance, and at the groups of Chinese, Japanese, and Europeans who passed back and forth in the streets. Hong Kong seemed to him not unlike Bombay, Calcutta, and Singapore, since, like them, it showed everywhere the evidence of English supremacy. At the Victoria port he found a confused mass of ships of all nations: English, French, American, and Dutch, men-of-war and trading vessels, Japanese and Chinese junks, sempas, tankas, and flower-boats, which made up so many floating parterres. Passepartout noticed in the crowd a number of natives who looked very old and were dressed in yellow. On going into a barber's to get a shave, he learned that these ancient men were all at least eighty years old, at which age they are permitted to wear yellow, which is the Imperial color. Passepartout, without exactly knowing why, thought this very funny.

19.2.oldText: On reaching the quay where they were to embark on the "Carnatic," he was not surprised to find Fix walking up and down. The detective seemed very much disturbed and disappointed.

19.3.oldText: "This is bad," muttered Passepartout, "for the gentlemen of the Reform Club!" He accosted Fix with a merry smile, as if he had not noticed that gentleman's chagrin. The detective did, indeed, have good reason to rail against the bad luck that pursued him. The warrant had not come! It was certainly on the way, but just as certainly it could not now reach Hong Kong for several days; and, this being the last English territory on Mr. Fogg's route, the robber would escape unless he could manage to detain him.

19.4.oldText: "Well, Monsieur Fix," said Passepartout, "have you decided to come with us as far as America?"

19.5.oldText: "Yes," returned Fix through his set teeth.

19.6.oldText: "Good!" exclaimed Passepartout, laughing heartily. "I knew you couldn't bring yourself to part with us. Come and engage your berth."

19.7.oldText: They went into the steamer office and secured cabins for four. The clerk, as he gave them the tickets, informed them that, the repairs on the "Carnatic" having been completed, the steamer would leave that very evening, and not next morning, as had been announced.

19.8.oldText: "That will suit my master all the better," said Passepartout. "I will go and let him know."

19.9.oldText: Fix now decided to make a bold move; he resolved to tell Passepartout everything. It seemed to be the only possible means of keeping Phileas Fogg several days longer at Hong Kong. He accordingly invited his companion into a tavern that caught his eye on the quay. On entering, they found themselves in a large, handsomely decorated room, at the end of which was a large camp-bed furnished with cushions. Several persons lay on this bed in a deep sleep. At the small tables arranged about the room some thirty customers were drinking English beer, porter, gin, and brandy, while smoking long red clay pipes stuffed with little balls of opium mingled with essence of rose. From time to time one of the smokers, overcome by the narcotic, would slip under the table, whereupon the waiters, taking him by the head and feet, carried him over and laid him on the bed. The bed already supported twenty of these stupefied sots.

19.10.oldText: Fix and Passepartout saw that they were in a smoking-house haunted by those wretched, cadaverous, idiotic creatures to whom the English merchants sell each year the miserable drug called opium, to the amount of one million four hundred thousand pounds—thousands devoted to one of the most despicable vices that afflict humanity! The Chinese government has tried in vain to deal with the evil through stringent laws. It passed gradually from the rich, to whom it was at first exclusively reserved, to the lower classes, and then its ravages could not be stopped. Opium is smoked everywhere, at all times, by men and women, in the Celestial Empire; and, once accustomed to it, the victims cannot do without it, except by enduring horrible bodily contortions and agonies. A great smoker can smoke as many as eight pipes a day; but he dies in five years. It was in one of these dens that Fix and Passepartout, in search of a friendly glass, found themselves. Passepartout had no money, but willingly accepted Fix's invitation in the hope of returning the favor at some future time.

19.11.oldText: They ordered two bottles of port, to which the Frenchman did ample justice, while Fix watched him with close attention. They chatted about the journey, and Passepartout was especially merry at the idea that Fix was going to continue it with them. When the bottles were empty, however, he rose to go and tell his master about the change in the time of the "Carnatic's" sailing.

19.12.oldText: Fix caught him by the arm and said, "Wait a moment."

19.14.oldText: "I want to have a serious talk with you."

19.15.oldText: "A serious talk!" cried Passepartout, draining the little wine that was left in the bottom of his glass. "Well, we'll talk about it tomorrow; I haven't time now."

19.16.oldText: "Stay! What I have to say concerns your master."

19.17.oldText: At this, Passepartout looked attentively at his companion. Fix's face seemed to have a peculiar expression. He sat back down.

19.18.oldText: "What is it that you have to say?"

19.19.oldText: Fix placed his hand on Passepartout's arm, and, lowering his voice, said, "You have guessed who I am?"

19.21.oldText: "Then I'm going to tell you everything—"

19.22.oldText: "Now that I know everything, my friend! Ah! that's very good. But go on, go on. First, though, let me tell you that those gentlemen have put themselves to a useless expense."

19.23.oldText: "Useless!" said Fix. "You speak confidently. It's clear you don't know how large the sum is."

19.24.oldText: "Of course I do," returned Passepartout. "Twenty thousand pounds."

19.25.oldText: "Fifty-five thousand!" answered Fix, pressing his companion's hand.

19.26.oldText: "What!" cried the Frenchman. "Has Monsieur Fogg dared—fifty-five thousand pounds! Well, there's all the more reason for not losing an instant," he continued, getting up hastily.

19.27.oldText: Fix pushed Passepartout back into his chair and went on: "Fifty-five thousand pounds; and if I succeed, I get two thousand pounds. If you'll help me, I'll let you have five hundred of them."

19.28.oldText: "Help you?" cried Passepartout, whose eyes were standing wide open.

19.29.oldText: "Yes; help me keep Mr. Fogg here for two or three days."

19.30.oldText: "Why, what are you saying? Those gentlemen are not satisfied with following my master and suspecting his honor; they must also try to put obstacles in his way! I blush for them!"

19.32.oldText: "I mean that it is a piece of shameful trickery. They might as well waylay Mr. Fogg and put his money in their pockets!"

19.33.oldText: "That's just what we count on doing."

19.34.oldText: "It's a conspiracy, then," cried Passepartout, who grew more and more excited as the liquor mounted to his head—for he drank without noticing it. "A real conspiracy! And gentlemen, too. Bah!"

19.36.oldText: "Members of the Reform Club!" Passepartout went on. "You must know, Monsieur Fix, that my master is an honest man, and that when he makes a wager, he tries to win it fairly!"

19.37.oldText: "But who do you think I am?" asked Fix, looking at him intently.

19.38.oldText: "Parbleu! An agent of the members of the Reform Club, sent out here to interrupt my master's journey. But, though I found you out some time ago, I've taken good care to say nothing about it to Mr. Fogg."

19.40.oldText: "Nothing," replied Passepartout, again draining his glass.

19.41.oldText: The detective passed his hand across his forehead, hesitating before speaking again. What should he do? Passepartout's mistake seemed sincere, but it made his design more difficult. It was clear that the servant was not the master's accomplice, as Fix had been inclined to suspect.

19.42.oldText: "Well," said the detective to himself, "as he is not an accomplice, he will help me."

19.43.oldText: He had no time to lose: Fogg must be detained at Hong Kong, so he resolved to make a clean breast of it.

19.44.oldText: "Listen to me," said Fix abruptly. "I am not, as you think, an agent of the members of the Reform Club—"

19.45.oldText: "Bah!" retorted Passepartout, with an air of raillery.

19.46.oldText: "I am a police detective, sent out here by the London office."

19.48.oldText: "I will prove it. Here is my commission."

19.49.oldText: Passepartout was speechless with astonishment when Fix displayed this document, whose genuineness could not be doubted.

19.50.oldText: "Mr. Fogg's wager," Fix went on, "is only a pretext, of which you and the gentlemen of the Reform Club are dupes. He had a motive for securing your innocent complicity."

19.52.oldText: "Listen. On the 28th of last September a robbery of fifty-five thousand pounds was committed at the Bank of England by a person whose description was fortunately obtained. Here is his description; it matches exactly that of Mr. Phileas Fogg."

19.53.oldText: "What nonsense!" cried Passepartout, striking the table with his fist. "My master is the most honorable of men!"

19.54.oldText: "How can you tell? You know scarcely anything about him. You entered his service the day he left; and he left on a foolish pretext, without trunks, and carrying a large sum in banknotes. And yet you are bold enough to maintain that he is an honest man!"

19.55.oldText: "Yes, yes," the poor fellow repeated mechanically.

19.56.oldText: "Would you like to be arrested as his accomplice?"

19.57.oldText: Passepartout, overcome by what he had heard, held his head between his hands and did not dare to look at the detective. Phileas Fogg, the savior of Aouda, that brave and generous man, a robber! And yet how many presumptions there were against him! Passepartout tried to reject the suspicions that forced themselves upon his mind; he did not want to believe his master was guilty.

19.58.oldText: "Well, what do you want of me?" he said at last, with an effort.

19.59.oldText: "See here," replied Fix; "I have tracked Mr. Fogg to this place, but I have not yet received the warrant of arrest for which I sent to London. You must help me keep him here in Hong Kong—"

19.61.oldText: "I will share with you the two thousand pounds reward offered by the Bank of England."

19.62.oldText: "Never!" replied Passepartout, who tried to rise but fell back, exhausted in mind and body.

19.63.oldText: "Mr. Fix," he stammered, "even should what you say be true—if my master is really the robber you are seeking—which I deny—I have been, and am, in his service; I have seen his generosity and goodness; and I will never betray him—not for all the gold in the world. I come from a village where they don't eat that kind of bread!"

19.66.oldText: "Consider that I've said nothing," said Fix; "and let us drink."

19.68.oldText: Passepartout felt himself yielding more and more to the effects of the liquor. Fix, seeing that he must at all hazards be separated from his master, wished to overcome him entirely. Some pipes full of opium lay on the table. Fix slipped one into Passepartout's hand. He took it, put it between his lips, lit it, drew several puffs, and his head, growing heavy under the influence of the narcotic, fell upon the table.

19.69.oldText: "At last!" said Fix, seeing Passepartout unconscious. "Mr. Fogg will not be informed of the 'Carnatic's' departure; and, if he is, he will have to go without this cursed Frenchman!"

19.70.oldText: And, after paying his bill, Fix left the tavern.

31.0.oldText: Phileas Fogg found himself twenty hours behind schedule. Passepartout, the unwitting cause of this delay, was distraught. He had ruined his master!

31.1.oldText: At this moment the detective approached Mr. Fogg, looked him intently in the face, and said:

31.2.oldText: “Seriously, sir, are you in great haste?”

31.4.oldText: “I have a purpose in asking,” Fix went on. “Is it absolutely necessary that you reach New York on the 11th, before nine o’clock in the evening, when the steamer leaves for Liverpool?”

31.6.oldText: “And if your journey had not been interrupted by these Indians, you would have reached New York on the morning of the 11th?”

31.7.oldText: “Yes; with eleven hours to spare before the steamer sailed.”

31.8.oldText: “Good—so you are twenty hours behind. Twelve from twenty leaves eight. You need to make up eight hours. Do you wish to try?”

31.10.oldText: “No; on a sledge,” replied Fix. “On a sledge with sails. A man has proposed such a method to me.”

31.11.oldText: It was the same man who had spoken to Fix during the night, and whose offer he had refused.

31.12.oldText: Phileas Fogg did not reply at once; but when Fix pointed out the man, who was pacing up and down in front of the station, Mr. Fogg walked over to him. A moment later Mr. Fogg and the American, whose name was Mudge, entered a hut built just below the fort.

31.13.oldText: There Mr. Fogg examined a curious vehicle—a kind of frame on two long beams, slightly raised in front like the runners of a sledge, on which there was room for five or six people. A tall mast was fixed to the frame, held firmly by metal stays, and a large brigantine sail was attached to it. The mast carried an iron stay on which to hoist a jib-sail. Behind, a sort of rudder served to steer the vehicle. It was, in short, a sledge rigged like a sloop. During the winter, when the trains are blocked by snow, these sledges make extremely rapid journeys across the frozen plains from one station to another. Carrying more sails than a cutter, and with the wind behind them, they skim over the surface of the prairies at a speed equal to, if not greater than, that of the express trains.

31.14.oldText: Mr. Fogg quickly struck a bargain with the owner of this land-craft. The wind was favourable—fresh, and blowing from the west. The snow had hardened, and Mudge was very confident he could carry Mr. Fogg to Omaha in a few hours. From there, trains run eastward frequently to Chicago and New York. It was not impossible that the lost time might yet be recovered; and such an opportunity was not to be turned down.

31.15.oldText: Not wishing to expose Aouda to the discomforts of travelling in the open air, Mr. Fogg proposed to leave her with Passepartout at Fort Kearney, the servant undertaking to escort her on to Europe by a better route and under more favourable conditions. But Aouda refused to be parted from Mr. Fogg, and Passepartout was delighted with her decision—for nothing could have made him leave his master while Fix was with him.

31.16.oldText: It would be hard to guess the detective’s thoughts. Was his conviction shaken by Phileas Fogg’s return, or did he still regard him as an exceedingly cunning rascal who, once his journey round the world was complete, would think himself absolutely safe in England? Perhaps Fix’s opinion of Phileas Fogg was somewhat softened; but he was nevertheless resolved to do his duty and to hasten the return of the whole party to England as quickly as possible.

31.17.oldText: At eight o’clock the sledge was ready to set off. The passengers took their places on it and wrapped themselves up tightly in their travelling-cloaks. The two great sails were hoisted, and under the pressure of the wind the sledge slid over the hardened snow at a speed of forty miles an hour.

31.18.oldText: The distance between Fort Kearney and Omaha, as the crow flies, is at most two hundred miles. If the wind held, the distance could be covered in five hours; if no accident occurred, the sledge might reach Omaha by one o’clock.

31.19.oldText: What a journey! The travellers, huddled close together, could not speak for the cold, which was made sharper by the rapidity at which they were moving. The sledge skimmed along as lightly as a boat over the waves. When the breeze swept low over the earth, the sledge seemed to be lifted off the ground by its sails. Mudge, at the rudder, kept it on a straight line and corrected, with a turn of his hand, the lurches the vehicle tended to make. All the sails were up, and the jib was arranged so as not to blanket the brigantine. A topmast was hoisted, and another jib, set into the wind, added its force to the rest. The exact speed could not be measured, but the sledge could not be going at less than forty miles an hour.

31.20.oldText: “If nothing breaks,” said Mudge, “we shall get there!”

31.21.oldText: Mr. Fogg had given Mudge a real stake in reaching Omaha within the agreed time, by the offer of a handsome reward.

31.22.oldText: The prairie across which the sledge was racing in a straight line was as flat as a sea. It looked like a vast frozen lake. The railroad that ran through this section climbed from the south-west to the north-west by way of Great Island, Columbus—an important Nebraska town—Schuyler, and Fremont, on to Omaha. It followed the right bank of the Platte River throughout. The sledge, shortening that route, cut a chord of the arc described by the railway. Mudge was not worried about being stopped by the Platte River, since it was frozen. The route, then, was quite clear of obstacles, and Phileas Fogg had only two things to fear—an accident to the sledge, and a shift or lull in the wind.

31.23.oldText: But the breeze, far from slackening, blew as though to bend the mast, which the metal stays nevertheless held firm. Those stays, like the strings of an instrument, resounded as if vibrated by a violin bow. The sledge slid along in the midst of a plaintively intense melody.

31.24.oldText: “Those chords give the fifth and the octave,” said Mr. Fogg.

31.25.oldText: These were the only words he uttered during the journey. Aouda, cosily wrapped in furs and cloaks, was shielded as much as possible from the assaults of the freezing wind. As for Passepartout, his face was as red as the sun’s disc when it sets in the mist, and he laboriously drew in the biting air. With his natural buoyancy of spirits, he began to hope again. They would reach New York on the evening, if not the morning, of the 11th, and there were still chances it would be before the steamer sailed for Liverpool.

31.26.oldText: Passepartout even felt a strong urge to seize his ally, Fix, by the hand. He remembered that it was the detective who had procured the sledge, the only means of reaching Omaha in time; but, held back by some presentiment, he kept his usual reserve. One thing, however, Passepartout would never forget, and that was the sacrifice Mr. Fogg had made, without hesitation, to rescue him from the Sioux. Mr. Fogg had risked his fortune and his life. No! His servant would never forget that!

31.27.oldText: While each of the party was absorbed in such different thoughts, the sledge flew on over the vast carpet of snow. The creeks it crossed were not even noticed. Fields and streams disappeared under the uniform whiteness. The plain was absolutely deserted. Between the Union Pacific railroad and the branch that links Kearney with Saint Joseph, it formed a great uninhabited island. Neither village, station, nor fort appeared. From time to time they shot past some phantom-like tree, whose white skeleton twisted and rattled in the wind. Sometimes flocks of wild birds rose, or bands of gaunt, famished, ferocious prairie-wolves ran howling after the sledge. Passepartout, revolver in hand, held himself ready to fire on any that came too close. Had an accident happened to the sledge then, the travellers, set upon by these beasts, would have been in the most terrible danger; but it held its steady course, soon outdistanced the wolves, and before long left the howling pack at a safe distance behind.

31.28.oldText: About noon Mudge saw by certain landmarks that he was crossing the Platte River. He said nothing, but he was certain he was now within twenty miles of Omaha. In less than an hour he left the rudder and furled his sails, while the sledge, carried forward by the great impetus the wind had given it, went on for another half-mile with its sails struck.

31.29.oldText: It stopped at last, and Mudge, pointing to a cluster of roofs white with snow, said: “We’ve got there!”

31.30.oldText: Arrived! Arrived at the station that is in daily communication, by numerous trains, with the Atlantic seaboard!

31.31.oldText: Passepartout and Fix jumped down, stretched their stiffened limbs, and helped Mr. Fogg and the young woman to step down from the sledge. Phileas Fogg generously rewarded Mudge, whose hand Passepartout warmly grasped, and the party set out for the Omaha railway station.

31.32.oldText: The Pacific Railroad proper has its terminus at this important Nebraska town. Omaha is connected with Chicago by the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad, which runs straight east and passes fifty stations.

31.33.oldText: A train was about to leave when Mr. Fogg and his party reached the station, and they had only just enough time to climb into the cars. They had seen nothing of Omaha; but Passepartout admitted to himself that this was no great loss, since they were not travelling to see the sights.

31.34.oldText: The train passed rapidly across the State of Iowa, by Council Bluffs, Des Moines, and Iowa City. During the night it crossed the Mississippi at Davenport, and by way of Rock Island entered Illinois. The next day, which was the 10th, at four o’clock in the evening, it reached Chicago, already risen from its ruins and seated more proudly than ever on the shores of its beautiful Lake Michigan.

31.35.oldText: Nine hundred miles separated Chicago from New York; but trains are not lacking at Chicago. Mr. Fogg passed at once from one to another, and the locomotive of the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Chicago Railway pulled out at full speed, as if it fully understood that this gentleman had no time to lose. It tore across Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey like a flash, rushing through towns with antique names, some of which had streets and tram-tracks but as yet no houses. At last the Hudson came into view; and at a quarter-past eleven on the evening of the 11th, the train pulled in at the station on the right bank of the river, in front of the very pier of the Cunard line.

31.36.oldText: The “China,” for Liverpool, had sailed three-quarters of an hour before!

32.0.oldText: The “China,” in leaving, seemed to have carried off Phileas Fogg’s last hope. None of the other steamers could serve his plans. The “Pereire,” of the French Transatlantic Company, whose admirable steamers are equal to any in speed and comfort, did not leave until the 14th; the Hamburg boats did not run directly to Liverpool or London, but to Havre, and the extra leg from Havre to Southampton would render Phileas Fogg’s last efforts pointless. The Inman steamer did not sail until the next day, and could not cross the Atlantic in time to save the wager.

32.1.oldText: Mr. Fogg learned all this by consulting his “Bradshaw,” which listed the daily movements of the transatlantic steamers.

32.2.oldText: Passepartout was crushed; missing the boat by three-quarters of an hour overwhelmed him. It was his fault, for instead of helping his master he had done nothing but throw obstacles in his path! And when he recalled every incident of the tour, when he counted up all the sums spent in sheer loss and on his own account, when he thought how the immense stake, added to the heavy charges of this useless journey, would completely ruin Mr. Fogg, he loaded himself with bitter self-reproach. Mr. Fogg, however, did not reproach him; and as he left the Cunard pier he said only: “We will consult about what is best tomorrow. Come.”

32.3.oldText: The party crossed the Hudson on the Jersey City ferryboat, and drove in a carriage to the St. Nicholas Hotel on Broadway. Rooms were taken, and the night passed briefly for Phileas Fogg, who slept soundly, but very long for Aouda and the others, whose agitation would not let them rest.

32.4.oldText: The next day was the 12th of December. From seven in the morning of the 12th to a quarter before nine in the evening of the 21st was nine days, thirteen hours, and forty-five minutes. If Phileas Fogg had left in the “China,” one of the fastest steamers on the Atlantic, he would have reached Liverpool, and then London, within the period agreed upon.

32.5.oldText: Mr. Fogg left the hotel alone, after giving Passepartout instructions to wait for his return and to tell Aouda to be ready at a moment’s notice. He went down to the banks of the Hudson and looked about among the vessels moored or anchored in the river, for any that were about to depart. Several had departure signals up and were preparing to put to sea on the morning tide; for in this immense and admirable port there is not one day in a hundred when vessels do not set out for every quarter of the globe. But they were mostly sailing vessels, which were, of course, of no use to Phileas Fogg.

32.6.oldText: He was about to give up all hope when he spotted, anchored at the Battery, a cable’s length off at most, a trading vessel with a screw, well shaped, whose funnel, puffing out a cloud of smoke, indicated that she was getting ready for departure.

32.7.oldText: Phileas Fogg hailed a boat, got into it, and soon found himself on board the “Henrietta,” iron-hulled and wood-built above. He climbed up to the deck and asked for the captain, who promptly appeared. He was a man of fifty, a sort of sea-wolf, with big eyes, a complexion of oxidised copper, red hair and a thick neck, and a growling voice.

32.11.oldText: “And I am Andrew Speedy, of Cardiff.”

32.12.oldText: “You are going to put to sea?”

32.19.oldText: “No passengers. Never have passengers. Too much in the way.”

32.21.oldText: “Between eleven and twelve knots. The “Henrietta,” well known.”

32.22.oldText: “Will you take me and three other persons to Liverpool?”

32.27.oldText: “No. I am setting out for Bordeaux, and I shall go to Bordeaux.”

32.30.oldText: The captain spoke in a tone that admitted no reply.

32.31.oldText: “But the owners of the ‘Henrietta’—” resumed Phileas Fogg.

32.32.oldText: “The owners are myself,” replied the captain. “The vessel belongs to me.”

32.37.oldText: Phileas Fogg did not betray the slightest disappointment; but the situation was a grave one. It was not at New York as it had been at Hong Kong, nor was the captain of the “Henrietta” the captain of the “Tankadere.” Until now, money had smoothed away every obstacle. Now money failed.

32.38.oldText: Still, some way had to be found to cross the Atlantic by boat—unless by balloon, which would have been reckless and was, besides, not practicable. Phileas Fogg seemed to have an idea, for he said to the captain: “Well, will you take me to Bordeaux?”

32.39.oldText: “No, not if you paid me two hundred dollars.”

32.45.oldText: Captain Speedy began to scratch his head. There were eight thousand dollars to be earned without changing his route—worth, surely, overcoming the repugnance he had for all kinds of passengers. Besides, passengers at two thousand dollars are no longer passengers, but valuable merchandise. “I start at nine o’clock,” said Captain Speedy, simply. “Are you and your party ready?”

32.46.oldText: “We will be on board at nine o’clock,” replied Mr. Fogg, no less simply.

32.47.oldText: It was half-past eight. To disembark from the “Henrietta,” jump into a hack, hurry to the St. Nicholas, and return with Aouda, Passepartout, and even the inseparable Fix was a brief job, and it was carried out by Mr. Fogg with the coolness that never left him. They were on board when the “Henrietta” was making ready to weigh anchor.

32.48.oldText: When Passepartout heard what this last voyage was going to cost, he uttered a prolonged “Oh!” that ran the length of his vocal range.

32.49.oldText: As for Fix, he said to himself that the Bank of England would certainly not come out of this affair well repaid. By the time they reached England, even if Mr. Fogg did not throw fistfuls of banknotes into the sea, more than seven thousand pounds would have been spent!

33.0.oldText: An hour later the “Henrietta” passed the lighthouse marking the entrance of the Hudson, rounded the point of Sandy Hook, and put to sea. During the day she skirted Long Island, passed Fire Island, and held her course rapidly eastward.

33.1.oldText: At noon the next day, a man went up onto the bridge to take the vessel’s position. One might have thought it was Captain Speedy. Not in the least. It was Phileas Fogg, Esquire. As for Captain Speedy, he was shut up in his cabin under lock and key, and was uttering loud cries that signified an anger at once pardonable and excessive.

33.2.oldText: What had happened was very simple. Phileas Fogg wished to go to Liverpool, but the captain refused to take him there. Then Phileas Fogg had taken passage for Bordeaux, and during the thirty hours he had been on board, he had so shrewdly worked with his banknotes that the sailors and stokers—who were only a temporary crew, and not on the best terms with the captain—went over to him in a body. This was why Phileas Fogg was in command instead of Captain Speedy; why the captain was a prisoner in his cabin; and why, in short, the “Henrietta” was steering her course towards Liverpool. It was very clear, from the way Mr. Fogg handled the craft, that he had once been a sailor.

33.3.oldText: How the adventure ended will be seen soon enough. Aouda was anxious, though she said nothing. As for Passepartout, he thought Mr. Fogg’s manoeuvre simply glorious. The captain had said “between eleven and twelve knots,” and the “Henrietta” confirmed his prediction.

33.4.oldText: If, then—for there were still “ifs”—the sea did not become too rough, if the wind did not veer round to the east, if no accident befell the boat or its machinery, the “Henrietta” might cross the three thousand miles from New York to Liverpool in the nine days between the 12th and the 21st of December. True, once arrived, the affair on board the “Henrietta,” added to that of the Bank of England, might create more difficulties for Mr. Fogg than he imagined or could wish.

33.5.oldText: During the first days things went smoothly enough. The sea was not very unkind, the wind seemed stationary in the north-east, the sails were hoisted, and the “Henrietta” ploughed across the waves like a proper transatlantic steamer.

33.6.oldText: Passepartout was delighted. His master’s latest exploit, the consequences of which he ignored, enchanted him. Never had the crew seen so jolly and quick-handed a fellow. He struck up warm friendships with the sailors and amazed them with his acrobatic feats. He thought they handled the ship like gentlemen, and that the stokers stoked like heroes. His talkative good humour infected everyone. He had forgotten the past, its vexations and its delays. He thought only of the end, so nearly accomplished; and sometimes he boiled over with impatience, as if heated by the furnaces of the “Henrietta.” Often, too, the worthy fellow circled around Fix, eyeing him with a keen, distrustful look; but he did not speak to him, for their old intimacy was gone.

33.7.oldText: Fix, it must be admitted, understood nothing of what was going on. The conquest of the “Henrietta,” the bribery of the crew, Fogg handling the boat like a skilled seaman, all amazed and confused him. He did not know what to think. After all, a man who began by stealing fifty-five thousand pounds might well end by stealing a vessel; and Fix was not unnaturally inclined to conclude that the “Henrietta,” under Fogg’s command, was not going to Liverpool at all, but to some part of the world where the robber, turned pirate, would quietly put himself in safety. The conjecture was at least a plausible one, and the detective began seriously to regret that he had embarked on the affair.

33.8.oldText: As for Captain Speedy, he kept up his howling and growling in his cabin; and Passepartout, whose duty it was to bring him his meals, courageous as he was, took the greatest precautions. Mr. Fogg did not seem even to know that there was a captain on board.

33.9.oldText: On the 13th they passed the edge of the Banks of Newfoundland, a dangerous stretch; in winter especially, there are frequent fogs and heavy gales of wind. Ever since the previous evening, the barometer, suddenly falling, had indicated a coming change in the weather; and during the night the temperature shifted, the cold sharpened, and the wind veered to the south-east.

33.10.oldText: This was a misfortune. So as not to deviate from his course, Mr. Fogg furled his sails and increased the steam; but the vessel’s speed slackened owing to the state of the sea, the long waves of which broke against her stern. She pitched violently, and this slowed her progress. Little by little the breeze swelled into a tempest, and it was to be feared that the “Henrietta” might not be able to hold herself upright on the waves.

33.11.oldText: Passepartout’s face darkened along with the sky, and for two days the poor fellow lived in constant fright. But Phileas Fogg was a bold mariner and knew how to maintain headway against the sea; he kept his course without even slackening his steam. When the “Henrietta” could not rise on the waves, she crossed through them, swamping her deck but coming through safely. Sometimes the screw lifted out of the water, beating its exposed end when a mountain of water hoisted the stern above the waves; but the craft always held straight ahead.

33.12.oldText: The wind, however, did not grow as boisterous as might have been feared; it was not one of those tempests that burst out and rush on with a speed of ninety miles an hour. It stayed fresh, but, unfortunately, it remained obstinately in the south-east, rendering the sails useless.

33.13.oldText: The 16th of December was the seventy-fifth day since Phileas Fogg’s departure from London, and the “Henrietta” had not yet been seriously delayed. Half the voyage was nearly accomplished, and the worst stretches had been passed. In summer, success would have been all but certain. In winter, they were at the mercy of the bad season. Passepartout said nothing; but he nursed his hope in secret and comforted himself with the thought that, if the wind failed them, they could still count on the steam.

33.14.oldText: On this day the engineer came up on deck, went over to Mr. Fogg, and began to speak earnestly with him. Without knowing why—a presentiment, perhaps—Passepartout grew vaguely uneasy. He would have given one of his ears to hear with the other what the engineer was saying. He finally managed to catch a few words, and was sure he heard his master say, “You are certain of what you tell me?”

33.15.oldText: “Certain, sir,” replied the engineer. “You must remember that, since we started, we have kept up hot fires in all our furnaces, and although we had coal enough to run at low steam from New York to Bordeaux, we do not have enough to run at full steam from New York to Liverpool.” “I will consider it,” replied Mr. Fogg.

33.16.oldText: Passepartout took it all in; he was gripped by mortal anxiety. The coal was running out! “Ah, if my master can get over that,” he muttered, “he will be a famous man!” He could not help passing on to Fix what he had overheard.

33.17.oldText: “Then you really believe we are going to Liverpool?”

33.19.oldText: “Ass!” replied the detective, shrugging his shoulders and turning on his heel.

33.20.oldText: Passepartout was on the point of vigorously resenting the epithet, the reason for which he could not for the life of him understand; but he reflected that the unfortunate Fix was probably very much disappointed and humiliated in his self-esteem, after having so awkwardly followed a false trail around the world, and let it pass.

33.21.oldText: And now what course would Phileas Fogg take? It was hard to imagine. Yet he seemed to have decided on one, for that evening he sent for the engineer and said to him, “Feed all the fires until the coal is exhausted.”

33.22.oldText: A few moments later, the funnel of the “Henrietta” was vomiting torrents of smoke. The vessel kept on at full steam; but on the 18th the engineer, as he had predicted, announced that the coal would give out in the course of the day.

33.23.oldText: “Do not let the fires go down,” replied Mr. Fogg. “Keep them up to the last. Let the valves be filled.”

33.24.oldText: Towards noon Phileas Fogg, having ascertained their position, called Passepartout and ordered him to fetch Captain Speedy. It was as if the honest fellow had been told to unchain a tiger. He went up to the poop, saying to himself, “He’ll be like a madman!”

33.25.oldText: A few minutes later, amid cries and oaths, a bomb appeared on the poop-deck. The bomb was Captain Speedy. It was clear he was on the point of bursting. “Where are we?” were the first words his anger allowed him to utter. Had the poor man been an apoplectic, he could never have recovered from his paroxysm of rage.

33.26.oldText: “Where are we?” he repeated, his face purple.

33.27.oldText: “Seven hundred and seven miles from Liverpool,” replied Mr. Fogg, with imperturbable calmness.

33.31.oldText: “—sir,” Mr. Fogg went on, “to ask you to sell me your vessel.”

33.33.oldText: “But I shall be obliged to burn her.”

33.35.oldText: “Yes; at least the upper part of her. The coal has given out.”

33.36.oldText: “Burn my vessel!” cried Captain Speedy, who could scarcely get the words out. “A vessel worth fifty thousand dollars!”

33.37.oldText: “Here are sixty thousand,” replied Phileas Fogg, handing the captain a roll of bank-bills. This had a prodigious effect on Andrew Speedy. An American can scarcely remain unmoved at the sight of sixty thousand dollars. The captain forgot in an instant his anger, his imprisonment, and all his grudges against his passenger. The “Henrietta” was twenty years old; it was a great bargain. The bomb would not go off after all. Mr. Fogg had taken away the match.

33.38.oldText: “And I shall still have the iron hull,” said the captain in a softer tone.

33.39.oldText: “The iron hull and the engine. Is it agreed?”

33.41.oldText: And Andrew Speedy, seizing the banknotes, counted them and slipped them into his pocket.

33.42.oldText: During this exchange, Passepartout was as white as a sheet, and Fix looked as if he were on the point of having an apoplectic fit. Nearly twenty thousand pounds had been spent, and Fogg was leaving the hull and engine to the captain—that is, almost the entire value of the craft! It was true, however, that fifty-five thousand pounds had been stolen from the Bank.

33.43.oldText: When Andrew Speedy had pocketed the money, Mr. Fogg said to him, “Don’t let this astonish you, sir. You must know that I shall lose twenty thousand pounds unless I arrive in London by a quarter before nine on the evening of the 21st of December. I missed the steamer at New York, and as you refused to take me to Liverpool—”

33.44.oldText: “And I did well!” cried Andrew Speedy; “for I have gained at least forty thousand dollars by it!” He added, more sedately, “Do you know one thing, Captain—”

33.46.oldText: “Captain Fogg, you’ve got something of the Yankee about you.”

33.47.oldText: And, having paid his passenger what he considered a high compliment, he was turning to go, when Mr. Fogg said, “The vessel now belongs to me?”

33.48.oldText: “Certainly, from the keel to the truck of the masts—all the wood, that is.”

33.49.oldText: “Very well. Have the interior seats, bunks, and frames torn down, and burn them.”

33.50.oldText: It was necessary to have dry wood to keep the steam up to the required pressure, and on that day the poop, cabins, bunks, and spare deck were sacrificed. On the next day, the 19th of December, the masts, rafts, and spars were burned; the crew worked with a will, keeping up the fires. Passepartout hewed, cut, and sawed with all his might. There was a perfect rage for demolition.

33.51.oldText: The railings, fittings, the greater part of the deck, and the top sides disappeared on the 20th, and the “Henrietta” was now only a flat hulk. But on that day they sighted the Irish coast and Fastnet Light. By ten in the evening they were passing Queenstown. Phileas Fogg had only twenty-four hours left to reach London; that was the time required to get to Liverpool, with all steam on. And the steam was about to give out altogether!

33.52.oldText: “Sir,” said Captain Speedy, who was now deeply interested in Mr. Fogg’s project, “I really feel for you. Everything is against you. We are only off Queenstown.”

33.53.oldText: “Ah,” said Mr. Fogg, “is that place where we see the lights Queenstown?”

33.56.oldText: “Not for three hours. Only at high tide.”

33.57.oldText: “We’ll wait,” replied Mr. Fogg calmly, without letting it show on his face that, by a supreme inspiration, he was about to attempt once more to overcome ill fortune.

33.58.oldText: Queenstown is the Irish port where the transatlantic steamers stop to put off the mails. These mails are carried to Dublin by express trains always held in readiness to start; from Dublin they are sent on to Liverpool by the fastest boats, and so gain twelve hours on the Atlantic steamers.

33.59.oldText: Phileas Fogg counted on gaining twelve hours in the same way. Instead of arriving at Liverpool the next evening by the “Henrietta,” he would be there by noon, and would therefore have time to reach London before a quarter before nine in the evening.

33.60.oldText: The “Henrietta” entered Queenstown Harbour at one o’clock in the morning, it being then high tide; and Phileas Fogg, after Captain Speedy had grasped him heartily by the hand, left that gentleman on the levelled hulk of his craft, which was still worth half what he had sold it for.

33.61.oldText: The party went ashore at once. Fix was greatly tempted to arrest Mr. Fogg on the spot; but he did not. Why? What struggle was going on inside him? Had he changed his mind about “his man”? Did he understand that he had made a grave mistake? He did not, however, abandon Mr. Fogg. They all got onto the train, which was just ready to start, at half-past one; at dawn they were in Dublin; and they lost no time in boarding a steamer that, disdaining to rise upon the waves, invariably cut through them.

33.62.oldText: Phileas Fogg at last disembarked on the Liverpool quay, at twenty minutes before twelve, on the 21st of December. He was only six hours from London.

33.63.oldText: But at this moment Fix came up, put his hand on Mr. Fogg’s shoulder, and, showing his warrant, said, “You are really Phileas Fogg?”

33.65.oldText: “I arrest you in the Queen’s name!”

34.0.oldText: Phileas Fogg was in prison. He had been shut up in the Custom House, and was to be transferred to London the next day.

34.1.oldText: When Passepartout saw his master arrested, he would have fallen upon Fix had he not been held back by some policemen. Aouda was thunderstruck by the suddenness of an event she could not understand. Passepartout explained to her how it was that the honest and courageous Fogg was being arrested as a robber. The young woman’s heart revolted against so heinous a charge, and when she saw that she could attempt nothing to save her protector, she wept bitterly.

34.2.oldText: As for Fix, he had arrested Mr. Fogg because it was his duty, whether Mr. Fogg were guilty or not.

34.3.oldText: It then struck Passepartout that he was the cause of this new misfortune! Had he not concealed Fix’s errand from his master? When Fix had revealed his true character and purpose, why had he not told Mr. Fogg? If his master had been warned, he would no doubt have given Fix proof of his innocence and satisfied him of his mistake; at the very least, Fix would not have continued his journey at the expense and on the heels of his master, only to arrest him the moment he set foot on English soil. Passepartout wept till he was blind, and felt like blowing his brains out.

34.4.oldText: Aouda and he had remained, despite the cold, under the portico of the Custom House. Neither would leave the spot; both were anxious to see Mr. Fogg again.

34.5.oldText: That gentleman was indeed ruined, and ruined at the very moment when he was about to attain his goal. This arrest was fatal. Having arrived at Liverpool at twenty minutes before twelve on the 21st of December, he had until a quarter before nine that evening to reach the Reform Club—that is, nine hours and a quarter; the journey from Liverpool to London was six hours.

34.6.oldText: If anyone, at this moment, had entered the Custom House, he would have found Mr. Fogg seated, motionless, calm, and without any visible anger, on a wooden bench. He was not, it is true, resigned; but this final blow failed to force him into any outward show of emotion. Was he being devoured by one of those secret rages, all the more terrible for being held in, and which only burst forth, with an irresistible force, at the last moment? No one could tell. There he sat, calmly waiting—for what? Did he still cherish hope? Did he still believe, now that the door of this prison had closed on him, that he would succeed?

34.7.oldText: However that may have been, Mr. Fogg carefully placed his watch upon the table and watched its advancing hands. Not a word escaped his lips, but his look was singularly set and stern. The situation, in any case, was a terrible one, and could be summed up thus: if Phileas Fogg was honest, he was ruined; if he was a rogue, he was caught.

34.8.oldText: Did escape occur to him? Did he check to see if there was any practicable way out of his prison? Did he think of escaping from it? Possibly; for once he walked slowly around the room. But the door was locked and the window heavily barred with iron rods. He sat down again and drew his journal from his pocket. On the line where the words “21st December, Saturday, Liverpool” were written, he added, “80th day, 11.40 a.m.,” and waited.

34.9.oldText: The Custom House clock struck one. Mr. Fogg observed that his watch was two hours fast.

34.10.oldText: Two hours! Granting that he was at this moment taking an express train, he could reach London and the Reform Club by a quarter before nine, p.m. His forehead slightly wrinkled.

34.11.oldText: At thirty-three minutes past two he heard a singular noise outside, then a hurried opening of doors. Passepartout’s voice was audible, and immediately afterwards Fix’s. Phileas Fogg’s eyes brightened for an instant.

34.12.oldText: The door swung open, and he saw Passepartout, Aouda, and Fix, who hurried towards him.

34.13.oldText: Fix was out of breath, his hair was in disorder. He could not speak. “Sir,” he stammered, “sir—forgive me—most—unfortunate resemblance—robber arrested three days ago—you are free!”

34.14.oldText: Phileas Fogg was free! He walked to the detective, looked him steadily in the face, and, with the only rapid motion he had ever made in his life, or which he ever would make, drew back his arms and, with the precision of a machine, knocked Fix down.

34.15.oldText: “Well hit!” cried Passepartout. “Parbleu! that’s what you might call a good application of English fists!”

34.16.oldText: Fix, who found himself on the floor, did not utter a word. He had only got his deserts. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout left the Custom House without delay, got into a cab, and in a few moments stepped down at the station.

34.17.oldText: Phileas Fogg asked if there was an express train about to leave for London. It was forty minutes past two. The express train had left thirty-five minutes before. Phileas Fogg then ordered a special train.

34.18.oldText: There were several rapid locomotives on hand; but the railway arrangements did not allow the special train to leave until three o’clock.

34.19.oldText: At that hour Phileas Fogg, having spurred the engineer on with the offer of a generous reward, at last set out towards London with Aouda and his faithful servant.

34.20.oldText: It was necessary to cover the distance in five hours and a half; and this would have been easy on a clear road throughout. But there were forced delays, and when Mr. Fogg stepped down from the train at the terminus, all the clocks in London were striking ten minutes before nine.[1]

34.21.oldText: Having made the tour of the world, he was behind-hand by five minutes. He had lost the wager!

34.22.oldText: [1] A somewhat remarkable eccentricity on the part of the London clocks!—TRANSLATOR.

35.0.oldText: The dwellers in Saville Row would have been surprised the next day if they had been told that Phileas Fogg had returned home. His doors and windows were still closed, and no sign of any change was visible.

35.1.oldText: After leaving the station, Mr. Fogg gave Passepartout instructions to buy some provisions, and quietly went home.

35.2.oldText: He bore his misfortune with his habitual calmness. Ruined! And by the blundering of the detective! After steadily covering that long journey, overcoming a hundred obstacles, braving many dangers, and still finding time to do some good along the way, to fail near the goal by a sudden event he could not have foreseen, and against which he had no defence—it was terrible! Only a few pounds were left of the large sum he had taken with him. All that remained of his fortune was the twenty thousand pounds deposited at Barings, and that amount he owed to his friends of the Reform Club. So great had been the expense of his tour that, even if he had won, it would not have enriched him; and it is probable that he had not sought to enrich himself, being a man who laid wagers for honour’s sake rather than for the stake itself. But this wager utterly ruined him.

35.3.oldText: Mr. Fogg’s course, however, was fully decided; he knew what was left for him to do.

35.4.oldText: A room in the house in Saville Row was set aside for Aouda, who was overwhelmed with grief at her protector’s misfortune. From the words Mr. Fogg let drop, she saw that he was meditating some serious project.

35.5.oldText: Knowing that Englishmen governed by a fixed idea sometimes resort to the desperate expedient of suicide, Passepartout kept a close watch on his master, though he was careful not to let it show.

35.6.oldText: First of all, the worthy fellow had gone up to his room and put out the gas burner that had been burning for eighty days. He had found in the letter-box a bill from the gas company, and he thought it more than time to put a stop to this expense, which he had been condemned to carry.

35.7.oldText: The night passed. Mr. Fogg went to bed, but did he sleep? Aouda did not once close her eyes. Passepartout kept watch all night, like a faithful dog, at his master’s door.

35.8.oldText: Mr. Fogg called him in the morning and told him to get Aouda’s breakfast ready, and a cup of tea and a chop for himself. He asked Aouda to excuse him from breakfast and dinner, as his time would be taken up all day in putting his affairs in order. In the evening he would ask permission to have a few moments’ conversation with the young lady.

35.9.oldText: Passepartout, having received his orders, had nothing to do but carry them out. He looked at his imperturbable master, and could scarcely bring himself to leave him. His heart was full, and his conscience was tortured by remorse; for he blamed himself more bitterly than ever for being the cause of the irretrievable disaster. Yes! If he had warned Mr. Fogg, if he had betrayed Fix’s plans to him, his master would certainly not have given the detective passage to Liverpool, and then—

35.10.oldText: Passepartout could hold it in no longer.

35.11.oldText: “My master! Mr. Fogg!” he cried. “Why do you not curse me? It was my fault that—”

35.12.oldText: “I blame no one,” returned Phileas Fogg, with perfect calmness. “Go!”

35.13.oldText: Passepartout left the room and went to find Aouda, to whom he delivered his master’s message.

35.14.oldText: “Madam,” he added, “I can do nothing myself—nothing! I have no influence over my master; but you, perhaps—”

35.15.oldText: “What influence could I have?” replied Aouda. “Mr. Fogg is influenced by no one. Has he ever understood that my gratitude to him is overflowing? Has he ever read my heart? My friend, he must not be left alone for an instant! You say he is going to speak with me this evening?”

35.16.oldText: “Yes, madam; probably to arrange for your protection and comfort in England.”

35.17.oldText: “We shall see,” replied Aouda, suddenly turning pensive.

35.18.oldText: Throughout this day (Sunday) the house in Saville Row was as if uninhabited, and Phileas Fogg, for the first time since he had lived there, did not set out for his club when the Westminster clock struck half-past eleven.

35.19.oldText: Why should he present himself at the Reform? His friends no longer expected him there. Since Phileas Fogg had not appeared in the saloon the previous evening (Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine), he had lost his wager. It was not even necessary for him to go to his bankers for the twenty thousand pounds; for his opponents already had his cheque in their hands, and they had only to fill it out and send it to Barings to have the amount transferred to their credit.

35.20.oldText: Mr. Fogg, then, had no reason to go out, and so he stayed at home. He shut himself up in his room and busied himself putting his affairs in order. Passepartout was continually going up and down the stairs. The hours were long for him. He listened at his master’s door and peered through the keyhole, as if he had a perfect right to do so, and as if he feared that something terrible might happen at any moment. Sometimes he thought of Fix, but no longer with anger. Fix, like everyone else, had been mistaken about Phileas Fogg, and had only done his duty in tracking and arresting him; while he, Passepartout. . . . This thought haunted him, and he never stopped cursing his miserable folly.

35.21.oldText: Finding himself too wretched to be alone, he knocked at Aouda’s door, went into her room, sat down, without speaking, in a corner, and looked ruefully at the young woman. Aouda was still pensive.

35.22.oldText: About half-past seven in the evening Mr. Fogg sent to ask whether Aouda would receive him, and a few moments later he was alone with her.

35.23.oldText: Phileas Fogg took a chair and sat down near the fireplace, opposite Aouda. No emotion was visible on his face. The Fogg who had returned was exactly the Fogg who had gone away; there was the same calm, the same impassivity.

35.24.oldText: He sat for several minutes without speaking; then, bending his eyes on Aouda, “Madam,” he said, “will you pardon me for bringing you to England?”

35.25.oldText: “I, Mr. Fogg!” replied Aouda, checking the beating of her heart.

35.26.oldText: “Please let me finish,” returned Mr. Fogg. “When I decided to bring you far away from the country that was so unsafe for you, I was rich, and counted on putting a portion of my fortune at your disposal; then your life would have been free and happy. But now I am ruined.”

35.27.oldText: “I know it, Mr. Fogg,” replied Aouda; “and I ask you in my turn, will you forgive me for having followed you, and—who knows?—for having, perhaps, delayed you, and so contributed to your ruin?”

35.28.oldText: “Madam, you could not stay in India, and your safety could only be assured by taking you to such a distance that your persecutors could not seize you.”

35.29.oldText: “So, Mr. Fogg,” Aouda went on, “not content with rescuing me from a terrible death, you thought yourself bound to secure my comfort in a foreign land?”

35.30.oldText: “Yes, madam; but circumstances have been against me. Still, I beg to place the little I have left at your service.”

35.31.oldText: “But what will become of you, Mr. Fogg?”

35.32.oldText: “As for me, madam,” replied the gentleman coldly, “I have need of nothing.”

35.33.oldText: “But how do you look upon the fate, sir, that awaits you?”

35.34.oldText: “As I am in the habit of doing.”

35.35.oldText: “At least,” said Aouda, “want should not overtake a man like you. Your friends—”

35.39.oldText: “I pity you, then, Mr. Fogg, for solitude is a sad thing, with no heart in which to confide your griefs. They say, though, that misery itself, shared by two sympathetic souls, may be borne with patience.”

35.41.oldText: “Mr. Fogg,” said Aouda, rising and seizing his hand, “do you wish, at once, a kinswoman and a friend? Will you have me for your wife?”

35.42.oldText: Mr. Fogg, at this, rose in his turn. There was an unwonted light in his eyes, and a slight trembling of his lips. Aouda looked into his face. The sincerity, rectitude, firmness, and sweetness of this soft glance of a noble woman, who could dare all to save him to whom she owed all, at first astonished and then penetrated him. He closed his eyes for an instant, as if to escape her look. When he opened them again, “I love you!” he said, simply. “Yes, by all that is holiest, I love you, and I am entirely yours!”

35.43.oldText: “Ah!” cried Aouda, pressing his hand to her heart.

35.44.oldText: Passepartout was summoned and appeared immediately. Mr. Fogg still held Aouda’s hand in his own; Passepartout understood, and his big, round face became as radiant as the tropical sun at its zenith.

35.45.oldText: Mr. Fogg asked him if it was not too late to notify the Reverend Samuel Wilson, of Marylebone parish, that evening.

35.46.oldText: Passepartout smiled his most genial smile, and said, “Never too late.”

35.47.oldText: It was five minutes past eight.

35.49.oldText: “For tomorrow, Monday,” said Mr. Fogg, turning to Aouda.

35.51.oldText: Passepartout dashed off as fast as his legs could carry him.

36.0.oldText: It is time to relate what a change took place in English public opinion when it came out that the real bank-robber, a certain James Strand, had been arrested, on the 17th of December, at Edinburgh. Three days earlier, Phileas Fogg had been a criminal whom the police were desperately hunting; now he was an honourable gentleman, mathematically pursuing his eccentric journey around the world.

36.1.oldText: The papers took up their discussion of the wager again; all those who had laid bets, for or against him, revived their interest as if by magic; the “Phileas Fogg bonds” once again became negotiable, and many new wagers were made. Phileas Fogg’s name was once more at a premium on ’Change.

36.2.oldText: His five friends of the Reform Club spent these three days in a state of feverish suspense. Would Phileas Fogg, whom they had forgotten, reappear before their eyes! Where was he at this moment? The 17th of December, the day of James Strand’s arrest, was the seventy-sixth since Phileas Fogg’s departure, and no news of him had been received. Was he dead? Had he given up the attempt, or was he still pursuing the agreed route? And would he appear on Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine in the evening, on the threshold of the Reform Club saloon?

36.3.oldText: The anxiety in which London society lived for three days cannot be described. Telegrams were sent to America and Asia for news of Phileas Fogg. Messengers were dispatched to the house in Saville Row morning and evening. No news. The police did not know what had become of the detective, Fix, who had so unfortunately followed a false trail. Bets, nevertheless, increased in number and value. Phileas Fogg, like a racehorse, was nearing his last turn. The bonds were quoted no longer at a hundred below par, but at twenty, at ten, and at five; and paralytic old Lord Albemarle even bet in his favour.

36.4.oldText: A great crowd had gathered in Pall Mall and the neighbouring streets on Saturday evening; it looked like a multitude of brokers permanently camped around the Reform Club. Circulation was impeded, and everywhere disputes, discussions, and financial transactions were going on. The police had great difficulty keeping back the crowd, and as the hour at which Phileas Fogg was due drew near, the excitement rose to its highest pitch.

36.5.oldText: The five antagonists of Phileas Fogg had met in the great saloon of the club. John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin, the bankers, Andrew Stuart, the engineer, Gauthier Ralph, the director of the Bank of England, and Thomas Flanagan, the brewer, were all waiting anxiously.

36.6.oldText: When the clock pointed to twenty minutes past eight, Andrew Stuart got up, saying, “Gentlemen, in twenty minutes the time agreed upon between Mr. Fogg and ourselves will have expired.”

36.7.oldText: “What time did the last train arrive from Liverpool?” asked Thomas Flanagan.

36.8.oldText: “At twenty-three minutes past seven,” replied Gauthier Ralph; “and the next does not arrive till ten minutes after twelve.”

36.9.oldText: “Well, gentlemen,” Andrew Stuart resumed, “if Phileas Fogg had come in the 7:23 train, he would have got here by now. We can, therefore, consider the bet as won.”

36.10.oldText: “Wait; let us not be too hasty,” replied Samuel Fallentin. “You know that Mr. Fogg is very eccentric. His punctuality is well known; he never arrives too soon, or too late; and I should not be surprised if he appeared before us at the last minute.”

36.11.oldText: “Why,” said Andrew Stuart nervously, “if I should see him, I should not believe it was he.”

36.12.oldText: “The fact is,” Thomas Flanagan resumed, “Mr. Fogg’s project was absurdly foolish. Whatever his punctuality, he could not prevent the delays that were certain to occur; and a delay of only two or three days would be fatal to his tour.”

36.13.oldText: “Observe, too,” added John Sullivan, “that we have received no word from him, even though there are telegraph lines all along his route.”

36.14.oldText: “He has lost, gentlemen,” said Andrew Stuart, “he has lost a hundred times! You know, besides, that the ‘China’—the only steamer he could have taken from New York to get here in time—arrived yesterday. I have seen a list of the passengers, and the name of Phileas Fogg is not among them. Even if we admit that fortune has favoured him, he can scarcely have reached America. I think he will be at least twenty days behind, and that Lord Albemarle will lose a cool five thousand.”

36.15.oldText: “It is clear,” replied Gauthier Ralph; “and we have nothing to do but present Mr. Fogg’s cheque at Barings tomorrow.”

36.16.oldText: At this moment, the hands of the club clock pointed to twenty minutes to nine.

36.18.oldText: The five gentlemen looked at one another. Their anxiety was becoming intense; but, not wanting to betray it, they readily accepted Mr. Fallentin’s proposal of a rubber.

36.19.oldText: “I wouldn’t give up my four thousand of the bet,” said Andrew Stuart, as he took his seat, “for three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine.”

36.20.oldText: The clock pointed to eighteen minutes to nine.

36.21.oldText: The players picked up their cards, but could not keep their eyes off the clock. Certainly, however secure they felt, minutes had never seemed so long to them!

36.22.oldText: “Seventeen minutes to nine,” said Thomas Flanagan, as he cut the cards that Ralph handed him.

36.23.oldText: Then there was a moment of silence. The great saloon was perfectly still; but the murmurs of the crowd outside could be heard, with now and then a shrill cry. The pendulum beat the seconds, which each player eagerly counted, listening, with mathematical regularity.

36.24.oldText: “Sixteen minutes to nine!” said John Sullivan, in a voice that betrayed his emotion.

36.25.oldText: One minute more, and the wager would be won. Andrew Stuart and his partners suspended their game. They laid down their cards and counted the seconds.
